Walker Subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computers and Society (cs.CY) A growing literature examines the impact of engaging with AI chatbots on our relationality: our ability to form relationships with others, maintain them through life's changes, and exit when needed. Currently, substantial work focuses on purpose-built AI companions (e.g. Replika, this http URL ), with less work investigating socioemotional uses of the more widely-used general-purpose chatbots. In this paper, we present a 100-person investigation into how people engage general-purpose AI for socioemotional needs. Participants' AI uses varied, from practicing specific social skills to seeking additional bandwidth and information as they navigated their social contexts. To explain this heterogeneity, we provide 8 states that describe how AI expands or contracts relationality for people with different levels of skills, bandwidth, and information. We then present a unified conceptual model for the role of technology in mediating human relationality, the Relational Capacity Framework, and outline future research designing appropriate roles for AI in human connection.

title: GeoJeV: Unified Spatial Probability for Training-Free Efficient Evidence Acquisition in Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing
text: Title: GeoJeV: Unified Spatial Probability for Training-Free Efficient Evidence Acquisition in Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing Xinyi Niu , Lingfeng Chen , Jiehua Zhang , Panhe Hu , Li Liu , Zhen Liu , Yongxiang Liu Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Signal Processing (eess.SP) Ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing imagery provides rich spatial details but poses challenges for accurate and efficient multimodal understanding. Existing evidence acquisition methods selectively explore relevant image regions, yet largely rely on generative multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for intermediate search control. However, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) primarily aligns these models with human-preferred responses rather than explicitly optimizing region-level relevance judgments, while repeated autoregressive decoding introduces additional computational overhead. To address these limitations, we propose GeoJeV, a training-free method that formulates evidence acquisition as spatial probability-driven decision making. At each evaluated region, a frozen JeV model produces a probability distribution over candidate regions. Specifically, Region Rank prioritizes candidate regions, Sparse Branch adaptively determines branching width through sparse probability support, and Depth Gate controls refinement depth based on branch sparsity and distribution concentration. By coordinating search priority, branching width, and refinement depth through a shared distribution, GeoJeV reduces reliance on RLHF-aligned generation and eliminates intermediate decoding. Experiments on LRS-GRO, MME-RealWorld-RS, and LRS-VQA achieve accuracies of 60.59%, 52.79%, and 34.32%, respectively. Across the three benchmarks, GeoJeV improves the average accuracy of Qwen3-VL-8B by +5.32pp with only 1.12 additional seconds per question, while achieving a 7.8-fold inference speedup over the recent method.

title: Learning to Restart: Differentiable Restart Policies for Optimization Dynamics
text: Title: Learning to Restart: Differentiable Restart Policies for Optimization Dynamics Yiman Fong , Zhonglin Xie , Zaiwen Wen Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) Adaptive restart mechanisms, which reset the momentum or other auxiliary state of an iterative optimizer, play a central role in the empirical performance of accelerated first-order methods, yet existing restart rules remain almost entirely hand-designed. The obstruction to learning restart policies is that, unlike the typical Learning to Optimize (L2O) setting, the discrete restart events make the resulting trajectory non-differentiable in the algorithm parameters and thus block gradient-based optimization of the restart policy. We resolve this obstruction by developing a differentiable framework for restart policies through their continuous-time limit. We introduce surrogate gradients for the restart events and optimization trajectories that are efficient to compute and provably converge to their continuous-time counterparts. We validate the effectiveness of our surrogate gradients in L2O settings, training restart policies that improve upon standard handcrafted adaptive restart criteria on quadratic and linear programs, and that transfer zero-shot from synthetic quadratics to logistic regression on real datasets.

title: Who's Asking? Audience-Conditioned Privatization
text: Title: Who's Asking? Audience-Conditioned Privatization Daniil Filienko , Anusha Bagalkotkar , Xan Vongsathorn , Sikha Pentyala Subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG) The abundance of user-generated conversational data makes the question of how to responsibly derive insights from confidential data without putting the individuals in it at risk ever more important. However, the majority of existing differentially private (DP) synthetic text generation (SDG) and anonymization approaches ignore the context of the data's downstream usage, which results in loss of important information. DP-SDG provides the same guarantee regardless of the recipient, and anonymization relies on predefined attribute categories. They both ignore the observation that an attribute that is harmless to one audience can be sensitive to another, and each audience typically needs only some attributes preserved. We propose Ext-Classify-Priv, a framework that (1) extracts the information types present in a corpus, (2) classifies which of them are private for a given audience following contextual integrity, and (3) protects only those attributes, using either anonymization or SDG with Feature-DP approaches. On Reddit data with 3 audiences, our audience-specific releases are more faithful than a single audience-agnostic release for every audience. On bioRxiv data, our SDG method improves MAUVE from 0.097 to 0.420 at epsilon=1 and on the proprietary real estate data, our anonymization method improves MAUVE from 0.698 to 0.959 over the best baselines.

title: Computer Vision by YOLOs for Detection of Major Diseases in Vietnamese Custard Apple Using Fruit Imagery
text: Title: Computer Vision by YOLOs for Detection of Major Diseases in Vietnamese Custard Apple Using Fruit Imagery Tri Nhut Do , Quoc Tuan Vo Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) Amid Vietnam rapid digital transformation in agriculture, the integration of artificial intelligence technologies for identifying, monitoring, and predicting crop pests and diseases has emerged as an inevitable trend.

title: Decoding spatial and semantic information from large-scale visual cortical activity for natural-movie reconstruction
text: Title: Decoding spatial and semantic information from large-scale visual cortical activity for natural-movie reconstruction Yukai Huang , Haoyu Albert Wang , Jiawei Zhang , Jialun Ma , Jiayao Ding , Yiran Lin , Xingyu Chen , Ziqi Gao , Yuguo Yu Comments: 24 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables; 11-page supplementary information included as ancillary file Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Neurons and Cognition (q-bio.NC) Reconstructing natural visual experience from cortical population activity is a central challenge in neural decoding, particularly for calcium imaging, where signals are noisy, temporally filtered, and paired neural-video data are limited. Here we present Ca2REAL (Calcium Activity to Reconstruct Events, Appearance, and Layout), a neural-to-video framework that conditions a pretrained video diffusion model through separate layout and semantic controls derived from calcium activity. Using measured responses from 7,863 V1 neurons in one mouse, Ca2REAL reconstructed held-out natural-movie clips with 81.4% all-pairs stimulus-identification accuracy, with its clearest gains over deterministic baselines in perceptual and semantic measures. We further evaluated the framework in a stimulus-aligned virtual population of 116,705 neurons assembled from encoding-model-predicted responses across 11 independently recorded datasets. Perturbation and ablation analyses showed that reconstruction depends on distributed, stimulus-specific population structure, with layout and semantic pathways providing complementary spatial and identity information. Temporal analyses further showed improved preservation of semantic dynamics across reconstructed clips. These results show that large-scale cortical population activity constrains the spatial, semantic, and temporal structure of natural visual experience, providing a generative framework for high-fidelity neural reconstruction of dynamic visual scenes.

title: Richness Is Not Evenness: Ordered Renyi Crossings under Self-Training
text: Title: Richness Is Not Evenness: Ordered Renyi Crossings under Self-Training Pranjal Srivastava Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) Recursive self-training of language models, a setting studied in model collapse, can reduce vocabulary while making frequent words, mostly function words, less dominant. We fine-tune English GPT-2 on its own output for nine generations, vary the training-data sampling temperature, and measure every model with one fixed sampler. As training temperature rises, Renyi entropy changes turn from loss to gain at distinct temperatures: min-entropy first, then collision entropy, Shannon entropy and observed richness. Between the outer crossings, word types fall while the most-common word becomes less dominant. Untruncated training at T = 1 lies in this interval: at 13,000 words, generation 9 has 24% fewer types than generation 0 yet collision entropy is 0.91 bits higher. The ordering persists with a finer grid, different measurement samplers, a fixed word budget and five fresh training seeds. Min-entropy again crosses before richness in four further settings (in Hindi only at interpolated roots) and in 12 of 13 distinct measurements under eight text representations. Next-token identities and a categorical simulation isolate decoding and sampling effects; the crossing order remains empirical. Fine-tuning on human text can produce the same split while likelihood improves, and no single order's sign reliably identifies worse likelihood across the tested settings. We recommend reporting entropy profiles at stated budgets with an independent quality measure.

title: Localizing and Editing the Goal Representation of a Vision-Language-Action Model
text: Title: Localizing and Editing the Goal Representation of a Vision-Language-Action Model Sudhanshu Srivastava , Faisal Aqlan Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) Operators can state safety constraints for robots as prohibitions such as "do not put the bowl on the stove". We study whether OpenVLA follows such prohibitions and where it represents the goal it executes. The 10 tasks of LIBEROGoal share one scene, so we can label the goal that each rollout executes. We combine closed-loop rollouts with activation patching, linear probes, activation steering and runtime monitors. On LIBERO-Goal, negation had no detectable effect on which task OpenVLA executed. The model executed the forbidden task in 79% of negated rollouts and completed 78% of plain tasks. A goal probe gives similar read-outs under "not X" and "X". Activation patching shows that the first action depends mostly on the instruction tokens before layer 12 and on the last prompt token from layer 16 onward. A fixed steering vector at the instruction tokens at layer 8 redirected 12 of 18 rollouts. Fixed vectors and prefill patches at layers 12 to 20 redirected none of 158. From layer 16, only patches at every decoded action token redirected the robot (15 of 18 rollouts at layer 24). When the instruction changes during a rollout, the layer-32 goal read-out detects non-compliance better than failure detectors, and an external probe on image and instruction features performs comparably. These results support enforcing prohibitions outside the instruction and monitoring goal read-outs against the specification. Goal edits in OpenVLA should act before layer 12 or patch every action token.

title: Segmenting Geometric Textures of 3D Meshes
text: Title: Segmenting Geometric Textures of 3D Meshes Weidan Xiong , Kaijie Qu , Shihao Feng , Shunqi Fan , Rongyu Xiong , Hui Huang Comments: Pacific Graphics 2026 Subjects: Graphics (cs.GR) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) Recognizing geometric texture patterns on 3D models is critical for applications such as heritage protection, model editing, and 3D printing. Existing 3D model segmentation methods predominantly focus on identifying high-level semantic parts, thereby failing to capture middle-level textures. While recent Vision-Language Models can perform image segmentation with appropriate text prompts, they still struggle to recognize 3D geometric textures. In this work, we present a method that segments 3D mesh models based on middle-level geometric textures. We further introduce a new geometric texture segmentation benchmark and fine-tune SAM3 accordingly. The segmented texture regions are then clustered based on DINO feature similarity and lifted from 2D to 3D. Additionally, we develop an interactive tool to enable both 3D model editing based on our segmentation results and model retrieval from the dataset based on geometric and texture similarity. Experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing methods in segmenting geometric textures and can facilitate various applications.

title: FATHOM: World-Model-Guided Diffusion Action-Trajectory Selection for Sparse-Marker AUV Tracking
text: Title: FATHOM: World-Model-Guided Diffusion Action-Trajectory Selection for Sparse-Marker AUV Tracking Xiaorui Wang , Zeyu Sha , Mingyang Yang , David Chen Wang , Feitian Zhang Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) Reliable relative tracking is fundamental to cooperative autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), yet remains challenging under nonlinear vehicle dynamics and degraded underwater visual conditions. Active light markers improve robustness to appearance variation, but provide deliberately sparse observations that can become incomplete or corrupted by occlusion, reflections, and detection noise during dynamic motion. To address the resulting partial-observation control problem, this paper proposes FATHOM, a world-model-guided diffusion action-trajectory selection framework for sparse-marker AUV tracking. FATHOM first integrates structured marker observations, inertial measurements, action history, and temporal dynamics into a predictive tracking belief using a multimodal task-supervised recurrent state-space model. A diffusion action prior then generates multiple expert-like multi-thruster trajectories, whose future tracking consequences are predicted through the learned latent dynamics. Rather than directly executing a generated trajectory, FATHOM selects the most favorable candidate under an explicit receding-horizon objective and continually updates the decision from onboard observations. Extensive offline analyses verify the learned predictive belief, multi-step world-model prediction, diffusion trajectory generation, and predictive selection. More importantly, comprehensive real-AUV experiments, including strong pose-based comparisons and component ablations, demonstrate robust autonomous tracking across nominal and challenging motions with naturally occurring partial marker visibility, while maintaining real-time onboard operation without motion-capture feedback.

title: Inside the Trap: A Renewal Law for Prefix-Cache Collapse in LLM Agent Serving
text: Title: Inside the Trap: A Renewal Law for Prefix-Cache Collapse in LLM Agent Serving Akshat Valse , Ali Jannesari Comments: 66 pages, 8 figures, 20 tables Subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC) ; Performance (cs.PF) Prefix caching lets an LLM agent's follow-up turns reuse cached KV, but a burst can tip an engine into a trap in which every turn misses and the backlog does not drain, at a load it served before. In registered paired tests on two engines, two GPUs and two models (passed at 9 of 10 rates), a 200-session burst left the engine at zero hits to the end in all 30 runs, while every matched no-burst run stayed good and a session cap prevented the trap in all 30 capped runs. We analyse an idealization of the trapped state exactly: for a fluid FIFO server on which every turn misses, we prove that along FIFO orbits its cycles obey a linear renewal recursion. As is classical, the trap drains if and only if arrivals are below the all-miss capacity; above it, a Perron root fixes the dynamics: every trapped state converges to a known self-similar regime in which the gap between turns grows linearly and the turns served are young and short. For our workload the backlog grows at 0.6 to 0.8 of the excess load and sessions complete faster than the all-miss capacity, a youth premium with turn-count and cost-growth factors, so in the model a trap's measured throughput overstates the recovery threshold. Retrospectively, with nothing fitted to trap data, the theory matches 57 stuck runs: the mean served prompt within 3% in 50 runs, completions above the all-miss capacity in every run, and the pooled gap growth. Blind in outcome, 4 runs trapped by a tool slowdown met 4 of 5 pre-set scores, cut traps persisted, and with a 20-step budget, trapped runs completed below the all-miss capacity, as predicted. Of two exits, refusing arrivals sheds sessions; a session cap restores reuse: in registered tests it rescued 9 of 9 established traps at the same load without shedding, and the engine stayed good after release. We do not prove that the engine converges to the model.

title: MotionCore: A Latent Neural Simulator for Video Generation with Rigid-Body Dynamics
text: Title: MotionCore: A Latent Neural Simulator for Video Generation with Rigid-Body Dynamics Zheng Wang , Zhengwei Gong , Yuanzhi Liang , Chi Zhang Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) Video generation models can produce highly realistic videos while generating physically inconsistent object motion. This limitation suggests that visual modeling alone may not provide a transferable representation of physical dynamics. We introduce MotionCore, a framework for learning physical dynamics via a learnable partial differential equation solver and focuses on rigid-body motion. We introduce a latent neural simulator learning to predict the evolution of object-level physical states from observed motion. Its predictions are then converted into spatially aligned latent controls for a controllable video diffusion model. The generator serves as a visual interface: it provides appearance and scene detail, while the learned dynamics model specifies the physical trajectory. To preserve this trajectory through the interface, MotionCore combines a diffusion-matching objective with a low-capacity decodability constraint on object identity and position. We evaluate MotionCore on public physical-consistency benchmarks and on paired data with known trajectories. Results indicate that MotionCore improves physical consistency and trajectory obedience in the evaluated rigid-body settings, while maintaining comparable visual quality. A controlled ablation protocol compares learned dynamics with an analytic prior and studies the choice of latent evolution processor.

title: From Procedures to Permissions: Learning Precise Subagent Authorization from Agent Skills
text: Title: From Procedures to Permissions: Learning Precise Subagent Authorization from Agent Skills Wenkai Yu , Ning Ding , Wentao Zhang , Yehui Tang Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) As language agents tackle increasingly complex tasks, they increasingly rely on multiple agents to coordinate specialized work, requiring decisions not only about what each subagent should do but also which tools and workspace resources it should access. Existing agent systems provide mechanisms for controlling tools and execution environments, but do not directly specify the resources required by each delegated subtask. Moreover, task outcomes and execution trajectories alone provide limited supervision for determining whether a subagent has received appropriate permissions. We observe that Agent Skills encode procedural knowledge describing the operations, tools, and files required at each step, providing a natural source of supervision for authorization. Building on this observation, we synthesize tasks and step-by-step procedures from Skills, execute them through subagent delegation in interactive environments, and use verified trajectories to construct training data for task execution and authorization. On ClawArena-Team, our method improves tool permission precision by 13.4 percentage points and workspace permission precision by 24.1 percentage points, while increasing overall task success by 11.6 percentage points for Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SkillsBench, our method remains competitive with existing agent data synthesis approaches. These results show that the procedural knowledge embedded in Agent Skills provides a source of supervision for precise subagent orchestration that task outcomes alone cannot provide.

title: Toward LLM Self-Play Under Data Scarcity: Effectiveness, Generalizability, and Trustworthiness
text: Title: Toward LLM Self-Play Under Data Scarcity: Effectiveness, Generalizability, and Trustworthiness Zhiyin Yu , Yuchen Mou , Bingzhe Wu , Zhonghai Wu , Shiyang Feng , Xiao Luo Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) has been driven largely by scaling model size and human-curated training data, yet this paradigm is increasingly constrained by data scarcity and diminishing returns from human supervision. Self-play offers a promising pathway for autonomous data generation and improvement, but current frameworks remain unsatisfactory due to a lack of a data-centric perspective, limited cross-domain generalization, and growing trustworthiness and security concerns. In this paper, we argue that real-world LLM self-play systems should achieve effectiveness, generalizability, and trustworthiness under data scarcity. To address these challenges, we outline three blue-sky research directions for future self-play systems: (1) data-centric self-play for effective experience generation, (2) generalizable self-play for open-world and unverifiable tasks, and (3) trustworthy self-play for reliable self-evolution. We further discuss research opportunities and solutions within each direction. This paradigm shift will establish a sustainable and safe AI ecosystem by transforming finite human knowledge into inexhaustible high-quality experience through self-play architectures.

title: Task-Contribution Dynamics of Adam in Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Slow-Manifold Analysis and Gradient Modulation
text: Title: Task-Contribution Dynamics of Adam in Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Slow-Manifold Analysis and Gradient Modulation Enzhan Zheng , Xiaoliang Song Subjects: Numerical Analysis (math.NA) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG) Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often suffer from imbalanced optimization of competing loss components, particularly when approximating solutions with high-frequency or multiscale features. Although existing balancing strategies have proven effective in alleviating this difficulty, the mechanisms governing the evolution of individual task contributions to Adam's parameter updates remain insufficiently understood. We introduce task-wise indicators to characterize this evolution and identify three distinct training regimes: smooth variation, intermittent spikes, and persistent oscillations. Focusing on the early smooth regime, we combine discrete-time analysis with a continuous-time singular perturbation framework under the full-batch setting and the parameter regime $(1-\beta_2)/(1-\beta_1)\ll1$. A first-order approximation of the locally attracting slow manifold reveals two factors governing the step-to-step redistribution of task contributions: curvature-related alignment disparities and differences in the coordinatewise distributions of preconditioned task gradients. Both factors involve Adam's shared second-moment estimate. Inspired by AdaTask, we propose Gradient-Modulated Adam (GMAdam), which modulates incoming task gradients using task-specific second-moment estimates. Numerical experiments on high-frequency Poisson and wave equations, the Allen-Cahn equation, and two-dimensional lid-driven cavity flow ($Re=100,400$) demonstrate consistent improvements in predictive accuracy over AdaTask at comparable computational cost.

title: Polarization calibration of fisheye cameras using skylight in the wild
text: Title: Polarization calibration of fisheye cameras using skylight in the wild Shuo Wang , Shiqi Che , Dianze Dong , Wenxin Liu Comments: 8 pages, 10 figures, submitted to ICRA 2026 Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) Skylight polarization provides directional cues for robotic navigation, but fisheye lens effects and analyzer imperfections can degrade polarization measurements across the field of view. We present a joint lens-analyzer calibration method that explicitly models incidence-dependent lens transmission together with analyzer gains and angular offsets in a unified eight-parameter formulation. Given known geometric calibration, rotations between camera frames can be estimated using visual features and cross-frame directional polarized light consistency can be used for polarization calibration. Therefore, our calibration approach requires only a short handheld outdoor sequence under natural skylight, without dedicated polarization calibration equipment or a predefined sky polarization model. On real-world outdoor sequences, the proposed method achieves a weighted cross-frame angle-of-linear-polarization (AoLP) mean absolute error below 0.5° across all incidence angles, with a 73.4% reduction in the 80°-90° incidence angle region, and generalizes to an independent sequence with an overall mean absolute error of 0.466° without refitting. Preliminary solar-azimuth experiments using a camera mounted on a quadruped robot further show improved alignment with the visible solar center, supporting the potential of calibrated AoLP measurements for relative-heading estimation and future polarization--inertial navigation. The calibration software tool will be released upon acceptance of this paper.

title: SSF-Net: A Spatial-Spectral Fusion Network for Accurate PDE Operator Learning
text: Title: SSF-Net: A Spatial-Spectral Fusion Network for Accurate PDE Operator Learning Siqi Zhao , Flora D. Salim Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) Machine learning methods for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) significantly improve computational efficiency over traditional numerical solvers such as finite element method (FEM). However, PDE dynamics inherently span both local and global dynamics: disturbances propagate and decay gradually through the domain, while global coupling effects can influence the whole system simultaneously. Capturing both types of dynamics with a low complexity model remains a key challenge. To address this, we propose the Spatial-Spectral Fusion Network (SSF-Net), built around a dual-branch Spatial-Spectral Fusion (SSF) block comprising a spatial branch and a spectral branch. The spatial branch employs a multi-directional Mamba, which mitigates its inherent causal, single-direction scanning bias and capture local interactions with reduced directional bias at linear complexity. The spectral branch leverages a Fourier transform with a block-diagonal MLP to efficiently capture global spectral features with reduced parameter count and complexity. The SSF block is embedded in a multiresolution convolutional encoder-decoder, which extracts multi-scale features. We evaluate SSF-Net on a comprehensive PDE benchmark spanning multiple task types and assess its long-horizon stability. Compared with attention-based and convolution-based baselines, SSF-Net achieves lower prediction error with fewer parameters while retaining near-linear asymptotic complexity in the number of spatial tokens.

title: HomeLoop: A Simulation Framework and Benchmark for Robot-IoT Coordination in Everyday Domestic Assistance and Safety
text: Title: HomeLoop: A Simulation Framework and Benchmark for Robot-IoT Coordination in Everyday Domestic Assistance and Safety Ramy ElMallah , Marc Bishara , Hyegang Kim , Yuxi Zhang , Chongyu Zhu , Chi-Guhn Lee Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) Recent progress in embodied robotics is bringing robots closer to deployment in homes, as vision-language models (VLMs) are demonstrating significant advances in reasoning, making VLM-driven robots promising home assistant agents. These agents will often be introduced into homes that already have cameras, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and residents with wearables. To fulfill their potential, they need to integrate with existing smart infrastructure and reason through ambiguous scenarios: a smoke alarm may come from a pan about to ignite, a pan already on fire, a resident cooking or a faulty sensor, and each calls for a different response. To that end, we introduce HomeLoop, a simulation framework and benchmark built on Isaac Sim that combines robot bodies, networked devices and wearables, simulated residents and visitors, faulty sensors, and hazards that evolve over time. Our benchmark is composed of 20 tasks across five families grounded in real-world household hazards and needs, and designed so that the same alert can have different causes. A runtime monitor scores each episode with temporal-logic checks on the final outcome and the actions along the way, and every action carries a predefined cost. We evaluate six open-weight and proprietary VLMs. The best achieves a family-balanced score of 61.9%, and across models we see a pattern of over-reaction: failed episodes involving prohibited interventions outnumber those involving missed required interventions by more than two to one, with models often shutting off the stove before investigating the alarm's cause. HomeLoop is an extensible foundation intended for use in research on robot-IoT coordination, long-term memory, proactive assistance, and privacy-safety trade-offs. HomeLoop will be released with 2,100 home layouts that can be automatically furnished in diverse configurations, five robot bodies and 20 networked device types.

title: On the Incompleteness of do-calculus for Universal Identifiability
text: Title: On the Incompleteness of do-calculus for Universal Identifiability Yaroslav Kivva , Aliaksandra Novik , Negar Kiyavash Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Probability (math.PR) We study the problem of causal effect identification from an arbitrary set of observational and/or interventional distributions, which we call Universal Identifiability (uID). The uID problem generalizes existing classical identifiability (ID) and general identifiability (gID) problems, which considered the identification problem from either mere observational distributions or a specific type of interventional distributions. Prior research has established graphical criteria to determine when a causal effect is identifiable in ID and gID problems. Moreover, algorithms that leverage do-calculus and basic probability manipulations have been proposed to compute these effects. Consequently, it has been shown that do-calculus is both sound and complete in these problems. Despite these well-established results, a formal definition of what it means for the do-calculus to be complete does not exist. We propose a rigorous formalization for the completeness of the do-calculus and show that the completeness results in previous work remain valid. However, for more general problems, such as uID, the rules of do-calculus are no longer complete. This is perhaps the reason why the uID problem has remained open thus far.

title: PRISM: Primitive Routing via In-context Skill Mixing for Retentive VLA Adaptation
text: Title: PRISM: Primitive Routing via In-context Skill Mixing for Retentive VLA Adaptation Jiachen Tao , Gengyu Zhang , Haoxuan Wang , Bing Liu , Yan Yan Comments: 19 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models promise a single language-conditioned policy adaptable to many manipulation behaviors, yet deployment additionally requires skill retention and long-horizon composition: a policy must retain previously acquired skills and reuse them inside composite tasks whose behavior changes across phases. The standard recipe absorbs every new task into one shared update, which provides neither a parameter-level locus for reusable skills nor a mechanism for invoking each skill along the trajectory. We observe that this missing structure is latent rather than absent: per-skill low-rank updates of a pretrained VLA occupy a robustly distinguishable, low-dimensional subspace, and a single composite-task LoRA concentrates roughly half of its Frobenius energy in this subspace, against a near-zero matched random-rotation control. Building on this geometry, we introduce PRISM, which represents reusable skills as parameter-level primitives: each skill family is stored as a dedicated low-rank action-expert adapter in a primitive bank, primitives are augmented with skill-specific low-rank residuals and composed at inference by a per-chunk VLM-conditioned router that reads the prefix representation to track task progress, and the router is supervised by per-chunk labels from a deterministic, task-conditioned, action-derived oracle. During composite training, the vision encoder, the language LoRA, the skill residuals, the router, and the shared action projections and time MLP are updated; every primitive is held frozen, so the base per-skill action-expert adapters are preserved by construction. On RoboCasa365, PRISM achieves 56.43% atomic-skill success and reaches 20.00% on long-horizon composite tasks, while a standard $\pi_{0.5}$-LoRA two-stage fine-tune reaches 17.86% atomic and 17.50% composite success. We additionally validate PRISM on an AgileX PIPER real-robot setup.

title: Composable Causality: A Toolkit for Systematic Time-Series Causal Discovery and Treatment-Effect Benchmarking
text: Title: Composable Causality: A Toolkit for Systematic Time-Series Causal Discovery and Treatment-Effect Benchmarking Muhammad Hasan Ferdous , Md Osman Gani Comments: 30 pages, 10 main text pages plus references and appendices, with figures and tables. Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets Track. Code and data at this https URL Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) Real-world multivariate time series rarely come with verified ground-truth causal structure, so research on time-series causal discovery and treatment-effect estimation depends on synthetic data. Existing tools are either fixed datasets that cannot be modified after release or script-based generators in which each script fixes one combination of mechanism, confounding, and missingness. Neither supports controlled experiments that vary a single property, such as sparsity, noise distribution, or missingness mechanism, while holding the others fixed. Counterfactual evaluation has the same gap, since existing simulators are built per paper with hardcoded mechanisms or produce observational data only. We introduce DTCD (Datasets and Toolkit for Causal Discovery), a data generation library that produces multivariate time series with ground-truth contemporaneous and lagged adjacency matrices. Topology, mechanism, noise, observational mask, and intervention policy are independent components that compose through configuration alone. Paired counterfactual twins, produced by caching the stochastic realization during the factual rollout and re-injecting it during the interventional rollout, recover individual treatment effects to numerical precision. A reference benchmark of eight discovery algorithms on eighty-one configurations and four treatment-effect estimators on eighteen configurations exposes failure modes that aggregate metrics hide. These include the inability of standard discovery methods to handle missing values, regardless of whether the missingness mechanism is informative, and a marginal-variance shortcut (varsortability) that we measure and remove by standardization. Code and data: this https URL

title: HOC2R: Hand-Object Contact Trajectories for Human-to-Robot Motion Transfer
text: Title: HOC2R: Hand-Object Contact Trajectories for Human-to-Robot Motion Transfer Hongkun Yu , Francisco M. López , Francisco Cruz Comments: 10 pages, 10 figures, 9 tables. Accepted for oral presentation at the Australasian Conference on Robotics and Automation (ACRA 2026) Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) Human videos contain abundant object-manipulation demonstrations, but they do not directly provide motion cues that a robot can follow. We present HOC2R, a Hand-Object Contact trajectory extractor for Robot motion that combines frozen DINOv3 and SAM 2.1 features with learned heads for hand-object association and contact localization. HOC2R supports two modes: count-aware automation that detects, counts, and localizes visible contacts in untrimmed videos, and fixed-two localization for two-finger grippers when contact frames are known. On a 30-task point-annotated benchmark, count-aware automation improves contact-count accuracy from 58.1% to 71.4% and reduces mean localization distance from 19.81 to 10.46 pixels relative to an adapted VRB2 baseline. On seven unseen RGB-D rollouts, a five-task fixed-two checkpoint reduces mean localization distance from 67.67 to 27.02 pixels. Across six robot evaluation sequences, the 30-task fixed-two checkpoint produces four feasible trajectories and succeeds on three tasks, compared with two feasible trajectories and one successful task for each adapted baseline. HOC2R is competitive in the evaluated single-hand scenes, robust to the hand-color shift, and strongest in the evaluated multi-hand scenes. These results support HOC2R as a practical pseudo-labeling method for extracting robot-usable contact trajectories from human demonstrations.

title: Frame: Form-Restricted Authoring with Model-Based Evaluation
text: Title: Frame: Form-Restricted Authoring with Model-Based Evaluation Nan Jiang , Mohammed Mohsin Hussain , Onkar Tiwari , Ankit Jain , Thong Q. Nguyen , Abhishek Agarwal , Vishal Chowdhary Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) Many professional reports reuse the structure of prior editions while updating the content. We formalize this setting as form-restricted report generation: given a sample report and new grounding documents, generate a report that preserves the sample's form while accurately reflecting the new evidence. We introduce FRAME, a benchmark of 120 EDGAR- and arXiv-derived instances across Financial Quarterly, Financial Annual, Academic Simple, and Academic Complex categories, built with a temporal three-snapshot pipeline. We evaluate outputs with three human-validated metrics: structural similarity via semantic tree-edit distance, coverage via information unit recall, and faithfulness via claim-level grounding verification. Across five LLMs, open-source models nearly match proprietary models on structure but lag on coverage and faithfulness; all models perform better on financial than academic reports, and performance declines with longer outputs and more complex grounding.

title: Glyph: An Interpretability Engine for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery in Clinical Data
text: Title: Glyph: An Interpretability Engine for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery in Clinical Data Robbie Holland , Ashwin Kumar , Mateus A. Esmeraldo , David Le , Andrea Fisher , Jiazhen Pan , Louisa Fay , Magdalini Paschali , Vasiliki Sideri-Lampretsa , Ates Fettahoglu , Stefania Moroianu , Philipp Wesp , Ivan Lopez , Tom Nuno Wolf , McKenzie S. White , Eduardo Pontes Reis , Fatima Rodriguez , Curtis P. Langlotz , Vasilis Syrgkanis , Imon Banerjee , Akshay S. Chaudhari , Sergios Gatidis Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) Automated scientific discovery has the potential to advance understanding of disease mechanisms and accelerate identification of early disease markers. Manual data annotation is infeasible at population scale, motivating methods that automatically extract pre-defined phenotypes in multimodal and unstructured clinical data. Such pre-defined feature sets determine and limit which associations these approaches can discover. This limitation extends to agentic AI systems that use these tools to query population-scale data. In contrast, foundation models (FMs) trained on large volumes of clinical data can perform tasks beyond their training objectives. This suggests their latent embeddings may represent novel or unexplored features that could yield insights into disease mechanisms, yet such latent features remain difficult to interpret. To address this challenge, we introduce Glyph, an automated multistage framework that extracts features from multimodal and unstructured clinical data using FMs and sparse autoencoders, interprets them as coded clinical concepts, and evaluates their value for clinical scientific discovery. We applied Glyph to abdominal CT volumes, CT radiology reports and laboratory measurements from 41,628 patients across different institutions. We identified 397 predictive concepts supported by 4,463 Bonferroni-significant associations. Moreover, a majority of discovered associations were automatically reproducible in held-out cohorts across different sites. Glyph concepts provided complementary associations to literature-derived markers, leading to gains in predictive power. We envision that interpretability can extend beyond a mechanistic understanding of neural networks to connecting implicitly learned features with clinical knowledge and establishing their significance for patient outcomes. We release Glyph at this https URL .

title: FANO: Anchored Forward-Noise Optimization for Diffusion Inverse Problems
text: Title: FANO: Anchored Forward-Noise Optimization for Diffusion Inverse Problems Shilong Han , Hongxia Wang Comments: 26 pages, 9 figures, 8 tables. Preprint, under review Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) Pre-trained diffusion models have become a widely adopted zero-shot prior for image inverse problems, among which annealed decoupling methods achieve leading reconstruction performance on nonlinear tasks. We find, however, that annealed methods that directly optimize the denoiser input $x_t$ exhibit radial drift in later layers: within-layer optimization drives the noise-component norm of $x_t$ away from its typical value, pushing the denoiser out of its high-performance regime and degrading reconstruction quality. To address this, we propose FANO (Anchored Forward-Noise Optimization). At each annealing layer, FANO fixes the previous denoiser estimate as an anchor and optimizes only the forward noise $e$, whose distribution is known, instead of $x_t$, thereby preserving the forward-diffusion structure of the denoiser input. The standard Gaussian prior on $e$ concentrates its norm near the typical value, and deviations degrade denoiser performance. We accordingly decompose $e$ in polar coordinates into a direction and a radial magnitude, and apply a soft potential to regulate the radius, keeping $x_t$ in the high-density region of the forward distribution. On multiple linear and nonlinear inverse problems, FANO matches the strongest current baselines on linear tasks and achieves consistent improvements on nonlinear tasks.

title: ResQAdam: Residual-Preserving Adaptive Optimization for Memory-Efficient Quantization Aware Training
text: Title: ResQAdam: Residual-Preserving Adaptive Optimization for Memory-Efficient Quantization Aware Training Liqun Ma , Shengkun Tang , Liangyu Wang , Lin Zhao , Wei Luo , Xinjun Niu , Spandan Tiwari , Ashish Sirasao , Kun Zhang , Zhiqiang Shen Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Computation and Language (cs.CL) Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top-r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r x r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%.

title: UAV-Based Computer Vision for Cattle Detection and Feed Bunk Spatial Analysis
text: Title: UAV-Based Computer Vision for Cattle Detection and Feed Bunk Spatial Analysis Pedro Oliveira Torrente , Diego Giaretta de Paulo , Lucas Pascotti Valem , Jianglong Yan , Everton Castelão Tetila , Jayme Garcia Arnal Barbedo , Liang Zhao Comments: 12 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Preprint of paper accepted in IEEE Transactions on AgriFood Electronics Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) Beef cattle production is central to Brazilian agribusiness and faces growing demands for efficiency, sustainability, and animal welfare. Precision Livestock Farming (PLF) offers tools to address these challenges, particularly through monitoring feeding-related spatial patterns in confined systems. Feeding management plays a decisive role in animal performance, yet its evaluation still relies largely on subjective, labor-intensive visual inspections that are hard to scale and prone to bias. This work proposes a computer vision framework based on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) to quantify cattle alignment and spatial dispersion at the feed bunk under real-world feedlot conditions. A UAV dataset was collected during flight campaigns at a commercial feedlot in Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil. Images were manually annotated into cattle head and cattle back classes to support object detection and image-level spatial analysis of cattle distribution. You Only Look Once (YOLO) models, namely YOLOv8 and YOLOv11, were evaluated, with YOLOv8 small used for the downstream spatial analysis. The feed bunk region was segmented using the Segment Anything Model (SAM), and geometric metrics based on detected head positions were developed to characterize alignment, spacing regularity, and clustering. The selected detector achieved 84.30% mAP50 and 35.50% mAP50-95, with an inference time of approximately 2.7 ms per image on an NVIDIA RTX 5060 Ti GPU. The resulting metrics distinguished representative regular and irregular spatial distributions by Root Mean Square Deviation - RMSD (1.06 m and 4.26 m), Coefficient of Variation - CV (42.70% and 96.31%), and clustering (0 and 2 clusters), respectively. These findings indicate that the proposed approach can provide indicators for assessing feed bunk spatial patterns in PLF.

title: Grid-Oriented Probabilistic Load Forecasting for AI Data Centers
text: Title: Grid-Oriented Probabilistic Load Forecasting for AI Data Centers Qingyi Yao , Ding Lin , Tianqiao Zhao , Meng Yue , Jianhui Wang Subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG) Probabilistic load forecasts for AI data centers need to represent both uncertainty under changing workloads and temporal dependence to support grid operations. This paper develops an open, grid-oriented benchmark using measured GPU power from a 448-GPU AI cluster. Forecasts are evaluated through four stages: probabilistic prediction, online uncertainty calibration, temporal scenario generation, and horizon-wide reserve sizing. Following a change in cluster utilization, a quantile LightGBM forecast achieves only 63.4% coverage for a nominal 90% interval, while online regime-conditioned calibration increases coverage to 87.3%. Even with well-calibrated marginal forecasts, independent sampling produces unrealistic ramp distributions and excessive reserve procurement. Reconstructing temporal dependence from historical forecast errors reduces the discrepancy in ramp statistics and lowers realized reserve cost by 7.4-10.6% across three forecasting tasks. These findings show that marginal forecast quality alone is insufficient for operational decisions and motivate joint evaluation of calibration, temporal structure, and decision outcomes.

title: Wellness Robots and the Path to Full Autonomy
text: Title: Wellness Robots and the Path to Full Autonomy Mohammad H. Mahoor , Matthew Hessler , Lombe Chileshe , Ola Alsaadi , Eshrat Emamian , Kerstin S. Haring , Richard M. Voyles Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) This paper introduces the autonomous wellness robot as a distinct category of socially assistive system, defined by its capacity to continuously assess and respond across the seven ICAA dimensions of wellness (see Figure 2). We propose the Care Robot Autonomy Scale (CRAS): a six-level taxonomy (L0-L5) modeled on the automotive automation standard SAE J3016 and evaluated across four wellness-aligned dimensions. We present Ryan, developed initially at the University of Denver and commercialized by DreamFace Technologies, as a case study. NIH/NIA-funded longitudinal evidence (N = 18; 887 hours) shows statistically significant cognitive improvement (SLUMS +2.61, p = 0.015) and a clinically meaningful directional reduction in depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 -2.50, p = 0.073), with no novelty effect. We position Ryan today at CRAS Level 1-2, with emerging Level 3 capabilities in some dimensions, and outline a three-phase roadmap to L5 (full autonomy) by the early 2030s.

title: LLM-Augmented Flow for Project Conformation and Task Complexity Evaluation Based on the TLM Framework
text: Title: LLM-Augmented Flow for Project Conformation and Task Complexity Evaluation Based on the TLM Framework Maksim Sysoev , Alexander Semenov , Ilia Cheshev , Alexey Gevorkyan , Danil Somov Comments: 5 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE) The software development process, from inception to a working product or solution, can be divided into two major phases: discovery (Discovery) and delivery (Delivery). The Discovery is further subdivided into High-Level Discovery (HLD) and Low-Level Discovery (LLD). During HLD, management identifies the business solution or product to be integrated into the company's infrastructure. LLD, in turn, produces requirement documentation artifacts, including the Product Requirements Document (PRD), Business Requirements Document (BRD), and Functional Specifications Document (FSD). Story Points (SP) are a widely used modern approach to measuring the effort required to accomplish predetermined tasks, and the artifacts listed above help derive SP more precisely. With the rapid growth of LLM technologies, one of the main questions that arises is whether the whole Discovery phase, or most of it, can be completed with the help of LLM tools. In this paper, we test a framework that structures requirement documentation generation and task complexity scoring, based on the model introduced by (Tran, Lévesque, and Meunier 2004) and executed with the help of agentic tools. The approach is applied to a real-world commercial project in the fintech domain as a feasibility study rather than a validation: development effort was not recorded for the tasks examined, and the resulting complexity scores are therefore reported as the output of the instrument rather than as validated estimates of effort.

title: ODD+LLM: Specifying LLM-Agent Behavior for Reproducible Social Simulation
text: Title: ODD+LLM: Specifying LLM-Agent Behavior for Reproducible Social Simulation Justin Downes , Robby Milletich , Newel Hirst Comments: 18 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. SocialAgent Workshop @ NeurIPS 2026 Subjects: Multiagent Systems (cs.MA) The ODD protocol is the de facto standard for describing agent-based models, but it lacks vocabulary for the components that determine LLM-agent behavior: prompt assembly, memory serialization, parsing, and retry logic. We propose ODD+LLM, a backward-compatible extension adding five documentation blocks grounded in the CoALA cognitive-architecture framework. To show that the gap matters, we conduct a multiverse analysis [Steegen et al., 2016] of a published LLM naming-game simulation, varying six specification choices a reimplementer must make. Variants that are defensible readings of the paper stay within statistical noise of our baseline reconstruction. Missing one instruction that the paper states but is easy to overlook (that the model answers as an outside observer rather than as a player) raises the share of runs settling on the convention agents individually favor from 0.35 to 1.00 and makes convergence three times faster, in a reimplementation that uses a different model from the original. We complement the demonstration with a reconstruction-sufficiency review of 28 published LLM-agent simulations, finding that the details of how prompts are built and how model outputs are parsed are undetermined in 77% of cases, and that no paper fully specifies its main LLM call. ODD+LLM gives the field a standard home for information it already produces but currently scatters across code repositories, supplementary files, and undocumented defaults.

title: DRAFT-Bench: Evaluating Frontier Agents Across the Professional Design Lifecycle
text: Title: DRAFT-Bench: Evaluating Frontier Agents Across the Professional Design Lifecycle Rong Pan , Jianqiang Wang Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) Can frontier general-purpose agents understand client intent, explore creative directions, execute revisions, and prepare production deliverables? We introduce DRAFT-Bench (Design Reliability Across Feedback and Tasks), a lifecycle-oriented evaluation of requirement elicitation, creative exploration, constrained editing, iterative revision, and production handoff. Its Requirement-to-Artifact framework links evolving requirements, protected properties, artifact versions, and delivery obligations. We compare native Codex/Astra and Claude Code across 35 design briefs under 43 conditions, alongside a separate 40-scenario RFQ track. Astra completes 43/43 design conditions and Claude 35/43. All scored core runs receive full structural credit, yet on the 28 core conditions scored for both systems, semantic checks flag violations in 11 for Astra and 5 for Claude; these are model judgments, not expert-confirmed failure rates. RFQ coverage is high, but success ordering changes across cohorts. SKU expansion, revision dependencies, and White ink files expose ambiguity among unmet obligations, missing inputs, and evaluator interpretations. These findings separate execution, requirement compliance, and professional acceptance. Unpaired tracks and different tools preclude claims of RFQ-to-delivery success, factory acceptance, or a pure model ranking.

title: SkinMind: Equipping Agentic RAG with Human-Inspired Graph Probing for Reliable Dermatology AI
text: Title: SkinMind: Equipping Agentic RAG with Human-Inspired Graph Probing for Reliable Dermatology AI Jing Hao , Weinan Zhou , Zhihong Lu , Yaling Shen , Yiming Xu , Yefeng Liu , Siyuan Yan , Shuaibo Li , Ming Dai , Junjun He , Zuyi Zhu , Jinjie Gu , Lijun Wu , Jian Wang Comments: 35 pages, 7 figures Subjects: Information Retrieval (cs.IR) Reliable dermatology AI requires access to verifiable evidence distributed across heterogeneous textual and visual sources. However, conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically relies on one-shot retrieval from flat corpora, limiting its ability to adapt retrieval granularity, explore multi-hop relations, and integrate multimodal clinical evidence. We introduce SkinMind, a multimodal agentic RAG framework that equips policy models with human-inspired graph probing for autonomous evidence seeking. SkinMind organizes retrieval as an iterative interaction between an orchestrator and a graph environment. Through eight hierarchical graph-probing tools, the orchestrator progressively identifies relevant entities, inspects node-level information, traverses relations and paths, and retrieves source-text and visual evidence. This progressive-disclosure design allows the model to adaptively determine the retrieval modality, exploration direction, and evidence granularity while constructing a query-specific evidence subgraph. To support autonomous graph probing, we construct SkinMind-KG from a 62M-token corpus of dermatology guidelines and textbooks and 423K images, guided by a dermatologist-informed schema and a conflict-resolution mechanism. The resulting graph contains over 1.0M nodes and 2.0M edges, unifying textual, relational, and visual evidence for retrieval. Across six dermatology VQA benchmarks and two policy-model settings, SkinMind improves the average score over direct answering by 8.70 and 8.89 points with GPT-5.4-mini and Gemini-2.5-Flash, respectively, while consistently outperforming competing RAG methods. Together, SkinMind and SkinMind-KG provide an effective foundation for evidence-grounded multimodal reasoning in dermatology.

title: Ordered Policy Optimization
text: Title: Ordered Policy Optimization Dongkyu Derek Cho , Pan Xu Comments: 36 pages, 12 figures, 11 tables. Published in Proc. of the 40th Conference on Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026) Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO); Machine Learning (stat.ML) Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) stabilizes policy updates by clipping the importance ratio between the new policy and the data-collecting policy. The standard rule uses one fixed clipping range for all samples. While this choice offers simplicity and effectiveness, it fails to distinguish statistically harmful extreme ratio values from large, yet tolerable changes. We study how to adapt the clipping radius to the reliability of the induced importance ratio distribution. Our case study demonstrates that reliable updates require controlling these extreme ratios, rather than merely verifying that individual ratios fall within a fixed interval. Motivated by this observation, we propose Ordered Policy Optimization (\textsc{OPO}). In each minibatch, \textsc{OPO} sorts the importance ratios, selects the extreme ratios that potentially have the largest effect on the update, and assigns them adaptive sample-wise radii instead of using the fixed clipping radius. These radii are derived from a prescribed tail profile, which specifies desired target values for the selected extreme ratios. The resulting objective remains first-order and requires only minibatch sorting and a modified policy loss. Experiments conducted on MuJoCo and Atari benchmarks demonstrate that this simple modification achieves strong performance relative to established baselines.

title: Surrogate Quality Score: A Novel Composite Performance Metric for Model Selection
text: Title: Surrogate Quality Score: A Novel Composite Performance Metric for Model Selection Maaz Ahmad , Iftekhar A. Karimi Comments: 22 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables Journal-ref: Ahmad, M., Karimi, I.A., 2026. Surrogate Quality Score: a novel composite metric for model selection. Computers & Chemical Engineering 215, 109864 Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Computational Engineering, Finance, and Science (cs.CE) The growing reliance on high-fidelity, state-of-the-art machine learning based models for engineering decision-making necessitates robust and systematic approaches for model selection. While high predictive accuracy at untrained points is a necessary trait in the final model, other attributes such as model complexity, forecastability, explainability, scalability, and physics-awareness may be equally important or relevant criteria depending on application context and user requirements. In this work, we propose a novel composite performance metric, Surrogate Quality Score (SQS) for model selection based on predictive accuracy and model complexity simultaneously. SQS heuristically integrates these two attributes through a weighted product of normalized measures, yielding a unified score to reflect overall model quality. A user-specified parameter in SQS enables explicit control over the accuracy-complexity trade-off, thereby incorporating human judgement and preference in the model selection process. We extensively discuss and justify the formulation of SQS and demonstrate its utility through an illustrative example. By combining predictive accuracy and model complexity, SQS offers a systematic and objective approach for model selection based on both attributes.

title: RevoSim: Scalable Multimodal Tactile Simulation for Dexterous Manipulation
text: Title: RevoSim: Scalable Multimodal Tactile Simulation for Dexterous Manipulation Ke Zhang , Lixin Xu , Ziyi Wang , Xiyue Dong , Jie Tan , Lianghu Shao , Xianpeng Wang , Chuanyu Li , Renjing Xu Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) We present RevoSim, a scalable and high-fidelity multimodal tactile simulator for the BrainCo Revo3 hand that jointly models 285 piezoresistive taxels and five visuotactile fingertips. RevoSim efficiently generates synchronized pressure, depth, RGB, and marker-displacement observations; on a single RTX 5090, its depth-conditioned marker-displacement configuration supports up to 4,096 parallel environments. We train in-hand manipulation and grasping policies entirely in simulation, establishing a foundation for future sim-to-real transfer. Project page: this https URL .

title: MESAM: Enhancing SAM2 for Few-Shot Segmentation through Semantic-Visual Memory Generation and Refinement
text: Title: MESAM: Enhancing SAM2 for Few-Shot Segmentation through Semantic-Visual Memory Generation and Refinement Tianyu Zou , Shengwu Xiong , Rui Wu , Ruilin Yao , Yi Rong Comments: 17pages, 12figures Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) This paper investigates how to leverage the powerful capabilities of the Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) to tackle few-shot segmentation (FSS) tasks. One major challenge lies in the substantial appearance differences between the support and query images, which may diminish the effectiveness of the memory-matching process in SAM2. Through systematic analysis, we find that the memory generated based on the categorical semantic information is robust to this appearance divergence and is more compatible with SAM2. Based on these observations, we propose a new Memory-Enhanced SAM2 (MESAM) method, which first introduces a Semantic-Visual Memory Generation (SVMG) module to separately construct a query semantic memory, a query foreground visual memory, and a support adaptive visual memory. Then, in our designed Interactive Semantic Memory Refinement (ISMR) module, we further enrich the obtained semantic memory with fine-grained visual details, and suppress its misatcivated background responses. Extensive experiments on the PASCAL-$5^i$, COCO-$20^i$, and LVIS-$92^i$ datasets demonstrate that MESAM consistently outperforms existing FSS methods, achieving new state-of-the-art segmentation performance. Our source code is available at: \href{ this https URL }{ this https URL }.

title: The Schur products of some nonbinary narrow-sense antiprimitive BCH codes
text: Title: The Schur products of some nonbinary narrow-sense antiprimitive BCH codes Haojie Xu , Xia Wu , Wei Lu , Xiwang Cao Subjects: Information Theory (cs.IT) In recent years, the Schur products of linear codes have been extensively studied due to their favorable applications in cryptography. In this paper, we aim to study the parameters of the Schur products of some nonbinary narrow-sense antiprimitive BCH codes. Let $\mathcal{C}_1$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$ be two narrow-sense antiprimitive BCH codes with designed distances $\delta_{1}$ and $\delta_{2}$, respectively, where $2\le \delta_{1},\delta_{2}\le n$. Let $\mathcal{C}_1\star\mathcal{C}_2$ be the Schur product of $\mathcal{C}_1$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$. We present some necessary and sufficient conditions for $\mathcal{C}_1\star\mathcal{C}_2\ne\mathbb{F}_q^n$ by applying some constraints to $\delta_{1}$ and $\delta_{2}$. Furthermore, we determine the dimensions of these products and lower bounds on their minimum distance. Several linear codes with best known parameters are found.

title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents
text: Title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents Jingdong Zhang , Jionghao Wang , Zhengming Yu , Yancheng Cai , Wei Chow , Chris Choy , Zhiyang Dou , Hang Hua , Jiachen Li , Zhixuan Liu , Chen Wang , Songlin Wei , Siyuan Yang , Yu Yuan , Xiaohang Zhan , Yucheng Zhang , Shuhong Zheng , Xin Li , Lingjie Liu , Wojciech Matusik , Zhengzhong Tu , Wenping Wang Comments: Project page: this https URL . Jingdong Zhang and Jionghao Wang contributed equally Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO) Frontier language models are increasingly deployed as agents, and how well an agent performs depends not only on its model but also on its harness: the prompts, tools, memory, and control loop through which the model acts. When an agent is applied to a new problem, a natural question is whether it can use the feedback of the task to improve the way it works, and not merely its answer. Most existing benchmarks keep the agent's harness fixed and score the solution it produces, or target large-scale model training. We introduce Flex-RSI, a benchmark for the recursive self-improvement of agents on vision and robotics tasks under a fixed budget. In each round, an executor improves the task solution, which is kept only if it scores higher on held-out validation data, and an improver then revises the harness, including the executor and itself. Every run starts from the same general-purpose harness, and the final solution is scored on hidden test data. Evaluating closed-source and open-weight models on tasks spanning perception, reasoning, robot action, 3D reconstruction, visual creation, and infrastructure, we find that self-improvement helps most when the agent builds its own solution, that feedback recording only success or failure holds back open-weight models, and that open-weight models fall furthest behind where outputs must pass strict checks of physical stability or exact correctness. Paired runs further show that editing the harness itself contributes to the gains.

title: More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow
text: Title: More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow Jianuo Shen , Pengyi Xu , Bo Zhang Comments: Accepted to AgenticAI4HPC 2026 (SC26 Workshops). 10 pages Subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Software Engineering (cs.SE) Translating parallel scientific codes between HPC programming frameworks is a critical but labor-intensive task. Existing LLM-based approaches rely on fixed sequential pipelines with undifferentiated repair strategies and correctness criteria that do not match scientific computing practice. We present an agent-skill framework that separates translation, compilation diagnosis, and execution validation into three autonomous agents coordinated by a verdict-driven orchestrator, routing each failure to a targeted repair skill rather than retrying blindly. An automated output check drives the self-correction loop, complemented by an offline LLM-based verification that exposes false positives escaping compiler and runtime checks. We evaluate the framework on 30 HeCBench kernels translated bidirectionally among CUDA, OpenMP, and SYCL with three open-source LLMs. Our framework attains the higher verified correctness rate in all 18 model and direction combinations over a state-of-the-art baseline while consuming up to 52.4% fewer tokens, remaining consistent across models and directions without architectural modification.

title: Age of Information for Power-Saving Devices with DRX Mechanism
text: Title: Age of Information for Power-Saving Devices with DRX Mechanism Hung-Chun Lin , Kuang-Hsun Lin , Hung-Yu Wei Comments: 6 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Published in IEEE ICC 2023 Journal-ref: ICC 2023 - IEEE International Conference on Communications, pp. 3234-3239, 2023 Subjects: Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI) ; Performance (cs.PF) Reducing the power consumption of User Equipment (UE) has always been a crucial issue in communication systems. As a result, Discontinuous reception (DRX) is introduced in today's New Radio (NR) networks as a power-saving strategy. In addition, the variety of low latency applications in 6G makes the issue of maintaining data freshness increasingly important. This paper aims to study the relationship between freshness and power-saving. To capture the information freshness, we use Age of Information (AoI) as the performance metric. To our best knowledge, unlike previous studies focusing on power saving and delay trade-offs, this is the first study considering the impact of DRX on AoI. We solve the closed-form solution of the peak average AoI with the DRX mechanism. Moreover, we propose a parameters adjustment strategy. Based on the simulation validation, our proposed strategy can enable the UE to keep the AoI close to the theoretical lower bound AoI while achieving high power-saving efficiency.

title: AIM: Adaptive Interaction in Multi-Agent Debate for Multimodal LLM Inference
text: Title: AIM: Adaptive Interaction in Multi-Agent Debate for Multimodal LLM Inference Wei Fan , JinYi Yoon , Bo Ji Comments: Accepted in The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026) Subjects: Multiagent Systems (cs.MA) Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) improves reasoning on multimodal tasks, but its accuracy and token efficiency depend on how agents interact during debate. A largely overlooked design choice is which interaction modalities agents use to exchange evidence. Existing methods rely on fixed text- or graph-based interaction, which fails to convey fine-grained multimodal evidence and thus degrades accuracy while inflating token cost due to verbose descriptions. To address this, we propose Adaptive Interaction in Multi-Agent Debate (AIM), an adaptive routing framework that dynamically selects the optimal modality combination for inter-agent interaction in multimodal MAD. Beyond text and graph, AIM introduces task-dependent modality interaction, where agents exchange targeted regions of interest from the task-specific multimodal input, such as image regions, audio segments, or spatio-temporal video clips. To determine the best combination for each instance, AIM first generates a structured baseline response and extracts interpretable routing features that capture which evidence the instance requires, how confident the baseline agent is, and how much new evidence each modality would add beyond the baseline response. A lightweight router then uses these routing features to select a modality combination that avoids both under-fusion (i.e., agents miss decisive evidence) and over-fusion (i.e., redundant modalities inflate token cost) risks. Across eight benchmarks spanning three multimodal task families, \name achieves the highest accuracy. Combining modalities improves accuracy by up to 6.4\% over the best single-modality baseline, and adapting the combination per instance adds up to 4.2\% over the most accurate fixed combination of each benchmark with up to 53.4\% fewer tokens.

title: MetricPose: Flexible 3D Human Pose Estimation with Depth and Geometric Cues
text: Title: MetricPose: Flexible 3D Human Pose Estimation with Depth and Geometric Cues Shifan Zhu , Sabad Modi , Hang Yang , Arushi Agrawal , Steven Gao , Meghan Huber , Nathan Wycoff , Donghyun Kim Comments: 9 pages, 3 figures, ICRA submission Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) In this paper, we present a 3D human pose estimator that predicts metrically accurate human joint positions in the camera coordinate frame. This task requires recovering the configuration of the body joints, scale, and metric camera-local placement. In monocular images, body size and camera distance are coupled through perspective projection and therefore cannot be determined uniquely from image alone. This ambiguity can be reduced by combining three complementary sources of information: learned RGB priors, direct depth measurements, and geometric constraints (e.g., ground contact) from the environment. We extend a pretrained full-body estimator with optional metric depth and geometry-processing modules that improve camera-distance estimation and depth-guided body refinement while preserving RGB-only operation. The resulting unified model supports RGB, RGB-Ground, and RGB-D using shared learned parameters. Unlike pelvis-relative error, camera-local error also measures placement relative to the camera. Compared with the existing foundation model SAM 3D Body, our methods with RGB, RGB-Ground, and RGB-D modes reduce camera-local joint-position error by 12.16%, 31.00% and 54.61% respectively.

title: Accuracy Is Not Value: Choosing Weak Supervisors by What the Student Inherits
text: Title: Accuracy Is Not Value: Choosing Weak Supervisors by What the Student Inherits Romano Li , Xunfan Cai Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) Weak supervisors are usually judged by their own errors, but what matters is what a student learns from them. For squared loss and any linear learner shared by all supervisors, we show that a supervisor's value is determined by its errors after they pass through the student's learning operator. Consequently, the inner products of the supervisors' raw errors can be compatible with every feasible value of the student's risk, and weighting supervisors by them can be arbitrarily worse than the best weighting in relative excess risk. This student-relative value is not identifiable from unlabeled data, but what is missing is small: one finite-dimensional projection of the target decides whether training on a weak aggregate helps, another decides how to weight the supervisors. Known teacher training rules, or a label-model condition stated in student-relative form, shrink it further. Clean labels close the remaining gap at a cost set by the geometry of the unresolved directions rather than by the dimension of the student's representation, with matching worst-case lower bounds. In Gaussian designs we also quantify when exact teacher structure beats ordinary stacking and when weak supervisors, combined with clean labels, beat every procedure that uses the clean labels alone. The guarantees extend to fitted ridge students and finite unlabeled data.

title: Region-aware error triage for medical image segmentation with groupwise conformal risk control
text: Title: Region-aware error triage for medical image segmentation with groupwise conformal risk control Nishi Kanta Paul , Md Shihabul Islam Shovo , Hoileong Lee Comments: 22 pages, 7 figures, 12 tables. Submitted to Biomedical Signal Processing and Control (BSPC) Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) Segmentation masks are increasingly reviewed rather than redrawn, which requires knowing where a mask is likely wrong. Learned error maps rank pixels by risk, but the number of pixels to warn is chosen ad hoc, and calibrating one warning threshold over all error pixels may leave errors far from the predicted contour under-flagged. We propose RACE-Triage, a post-hoc error triage framework that leaves the segmentation mask unchanged. A risk network is trained on out-of-fold predictions from backbone-independent inputs. The predicted contour partitions each image into a boundary band and a non-boundary region, and conformal risk control is applied separately in each region to bound the expected fraction of missed errors among cases with errors there. On ISIC 2018 dermoscopy and BUSI breast ultrasound (where patient identifiers are unavailable, so independence across images is assumed), pooled control met its overall target but missed on average 31.8% and 36.4% of non-boundary errors. Regional control reduced these fractions to 19.3% and 20.9% and raised the recall of size-filtered false-negative components from 0.722 to 0.818 and from 0.611 to 0.763. The mean warned area grew by 1.6 and 4.9 percentage points, and its 95th percentile reached 23.5% and 38.5%. The effect held across three seeds and a second backbone, and area-matched heuristics did not reproduce it. On the external PH$^2$ set, frozen thresholds exceeded both targets, whereas recalibration with 100 local images brought the mean over repeated splits below them. Regional calibration improves non-boundary error coverage at a measured increase in warned area.

title: Global Sinkhorn Convergence and Spectral Stability of Matrix Scaling
text: Title: Global Sinkhorn Convergence and Spectral Stability of Matrix Scaling Kun He Comments: 71 pages Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS) We give a global spectral bound for the Sinkhorn--Knopp (SK) algorithm. Let $A$ be a row-stochastic nonnegative $n\times n$ matrix admitting a finite doubly stochastic scaling $B$. Define \[ g=1-s_2(B)^2>0, \qquad D=\min\left\{\|(u,v)\|_\infty: B=\operatorname{diag}(e^u)A\operatorname{diag}(e^{-v})\right\}. \] From the standard initialization, SK achieves total marginal $\ell_1$ error $\varepsilon$ in \[ O\!\left(\frac{D+\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon)}{g}\right) \] iterations. A scale-invariant potential contracts globally according to the spectrum of $B$. The linear dependence on $D$ is necessary in the fixed-gap regime: we construct strictly positive inputs with constant input and endpoint spectral gaps, $D=\Theta(n)$, and an $\Omega(n)$ iteration lower bound at error $n^{-2}$. Our upper bound gives $O(n)$ iterations on this family. We next give spectral certificates for scalability and short scaling distance. For a row-stochastic input $A$ with positive column sums $c_j$, set \[ K=\frac{\max_jc_j}{\min_jc_j},\qquad \sigma=s_2\!\left(A\operatorname{diag}(c)^{-1/2}\right). \] The input-only condition $\sqrt K\,\sigma<1$ certifies exact scalability and polynomial scaling distortion, with $D=O(\log n)$ for fixed $K$ and a fixed positive spectral margin. Given a finite scaling $B$, the weaker condition $\sqrt K\,\sigma s_2(B)<1$ gives the same structural bounds. With a constant endpoint gap, these bounds imply logarithmic SK iteration complexity. Boundary constructions show that the strict spectral inequalities cannot uniformly be replaced by nonstrict ones.

title: Concordance-Optimal Continuous Music Emotion Estimation: Variance Decomposition, Dual-Branch Temporal Fusion, and Conformal Prediction Intervals
